ee:2012:q1.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 1
ee:2012:q1.question:
Two independent random variables X and Y are uniformly distributed in the
interval [-1,1]. The probability that max [X,Y] is less than 1/2 is

detailed_solution.markdown: $-1 \leq x\leq 1 \text{ and } -1 \leq y\leq 1$ is the entire rectangle.The region in which maximum of {x,y} is less than 1/2 is shown below as shaded regioninside this rectangle. $$\begin{aligned} P\left ( max{x,y} \lt \frac{1}{2} \right )&=\frac{\text{Area of shaded region}}{\text{Area of entire rectangle}} \\ &= \frac{\frac{3}{2} \times \frac{3}{2}}{2 \times 2}=\frac{9}{16} \end{aligned}$$ Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

ee:2012:q2.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 2
ee:2012:q2.question: If $x = \sqrt{-1}$, then the value of $x^{x}$ is

detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=i, \text{ then in polar coordinates,} \\ x &=\cos \frac{\pi}{2} +i \sin \frac{\pi}{2}=e^{\frac{\pi}{2}i}\\ \text{Now, } x^x&=i^i =(e^{\frac{\pi}{2}i})^i=e^{i^2 \frac{\pi}{2}}=e^{-\frac{\pi}{2}} \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

ee:2012:q3.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 3
ee:2012:q3.question: Given $f(z)=\frac{1}{z+1}-\frac{2}{z+3}$. If C is a counter clockwise path in the z-plane such that |z+1|=1, the value of $\frac{1}{2 \pi j}\oint_{C}f(z)dz$ is

detailed_solution.markdown: Given: $$\begin{aligned} f(z)&=\frac{1}{z+1}-\frac{2}{z+3}\\ &=\frac{(Z+3)-2(Z+1)}{(Z+1)(Z+3)}\\ &=\frac{-Z+1}{(Z+1)(Z+3)} \end{aligned}$$ Poles are at -1 and -3 i.e. (-1,0) and (-3,0). From figure below of |Z+1|=1, we see that (-1,0) is inside the circle and (-3,0) is outside the circle. Residue theorem says, $\frac{1}{2 \pi j}\oint _Cf(z)dz=$Residue of those poles which are inside C. So the required integral $\frac{1}{2 \pi j}\oint _Cf(z)dz$ is given by the residue of function at poles (-1,0) ( which is inside the circle). This residue is $=\frac{-(-1)+1}{(-1+3)}=\frac{2}{2}=1$ Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

ee:2012:q6.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 6
ee:2012:q6.question:
A system with transfer function
$G(s)=\frac{(s^{2}+9)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)}$
is excited by $sin(\omega t)$ . The steady-state output of the system is zero at

detailed_solution.markdown:
Fpr sinusoidal excitation,

$s=j\omega$

$\therefore \;\;G(j\omega )=\frac{(-\omega ^2+9)(j\omega +2)}{(j\omega +1)(j\omega +3)(j\omega +4)}$

For zero steady state output

$|G(j\omega )|=0$

$\;\;\;=\frac{(-\omega ^2+9)\sqrt{\omega ^2+4}}{(\omega ^2+1)(\sqrt{\omega ^2+9})(\sqrt{\omega ^2+16})}$

For zero steady state output,

$\Rightarrow \; \omega ^2=9$

$\Rightarrow \; \omega =3 \; rad/sec$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

ee:2012:q8.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 8
ee:2012:q8.question: If $x[n] = (1/3)^{|n|}-(1/2)^{n} u[n]$, then the region of convergence (ROC) of its Z-transform in the Z-plane will be

ee:2012:q11.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 11
ee:2012:q11.question: A two-phase load draws the following phase currents : $i_{1}(t)=I_{m}sin(\omega t-\phi _{1})$, $i_{2}(t)=I_{m}cos(\omega t-\phi _{2})$. These currents are balanced if $\phi _{1}$ is equal to.

detailed_solution.markdown:
In two phase, current are balanced if phase difference is $90^{\circ}$.

$i_1(t)=I_m \sin (\omega t-\phi _1)$

$i_2(t)=I_m \sin (\omega t-\phi _2+90^{\circ})$

Phase difference is $90^{\circ},$

$\omega t-\phi _2+90^{\circ}-(\omega t-\phi _1)=90^{\circ}$

$\phi _1-\phi _2=0$

$\phi _1=\phi _2$

Therefore, the correct answer is **D**.

ee:2012:q14.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 14
ee:2012:q14.question: With initial condition x(1)=0.5, the solution of the differential equation $t\frac{dx}{dt}+x=t$, is

detailed_solution.markdown:
The given differential equation is $\frac{tdx}{dt}+x=t$ with initial condition $x(t)=\frac{1}{2}$ which is same as  $\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{x}{t}=1$

Which is a linear differential equation

$\frac{dx}{dt}+P{x}=Q$

Where,  $P=\frac{1}{t}$ and Q=1

Integrating factor $=e^{\int P\;dt}=e^{\int \frac{1}{t}dt}=e^{\log _{e}t}=t$

Solution  is

$$\begin{aligned} x\cdot (IF) &=\int Q\cdot (IF)dt +C\\ x\cdot t&= \int 1\cdot t\cdot dt+C\\ xt&= \frac{t^2}{2}+C\\ x&= \frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t}\\ \text{Put } x(1)&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; C&=0 \\ \text{So, }x&=\frac{t}{2}\text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **D**.

ee:2012:q15.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 15
ee:2012:q15.question: The unilateral Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is $\frac{1}{s^{2}+s+1}$. The unilateral Laplace transform of $tf(t)$ is

detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{If }L[f(t)]&=\bar{f}(s)\\ \text{then, }L[t^nf(t)]&=(-1)^n\frac{d^n}{ds^n}\bar{f}(s)\\ &\text{In this problem,}\\ \text{Given, }L[f(t)]&=\frac{1}{s^2+s+1}=\bar{f}(s)\\ &\text{We need,}\\ L[tf(t)]&=(-1)^n\frac{d^1}{ds^1}\bar{f}(s)\\ &=-\frac{d}{ds}\bar{f}(s)\\ &=-\frac{d}{ds}\left [ \frac{1}{s^2+s+1} \right ]\\ &=-\left [ \frac{-1}{(s^2+s+1)^2} \right ] \times (2s+1)\\ &=\frac{2s+1}{(s^2+s+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **D**.

ee:2012:q21.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 21
ee:2012:q21.question:
The figure shows a two-generator system applying a load of $P_D$= 40MW, connected at bus 2.

The fuel cost of generators G1 and G2 are :
$C_1(P_{G1})$=10,000 Rs/MWh and $C_2(P_{G2})$=12,500 Rs/MWh and the loss in the line is $P_{loass(pu)}=0.5P_{G1(pu)}^2$, where the loss coefficient is specified in pu on a 100 MVA base. The most economic power generation schedule in MW is

primary.subtopicLabel: Economic Power Generation and Load Dispatch

detailed_solution.concept: Power Systems - Economic Power Generation and Load Dispatch
detailed_solution.markdown:
From cordination equation

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{dF_n}{dP_{Gn}}\cdot \frac{1}{1-\frac{\partial P_L}{\partial P_{Gn}}}&=\lambda \\ \text{Given: }P_L&=0.5P_{G1}^2\\ \frac{\partial P_L}{\partial P_{G1}}=P_{G1} \text{ and } \frac{\partial P_L}{\partial P_{G2}}&= 0\\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{dF_{1}}{dP_{G1}}\frac{1}{1-P_{G1}}&=\frac{dF_2}{dP_{G2}}\frac{1}{1-0}\\ \Rightarrow \; 10000 \times \frac{1}{1-P_{G1}}&=12500\\ 1-P_{G1}=\frac{100}{125}&=\frac{4}{5}\\ P_{G1}&=\frac{1}{5}p.u.\\ \end{aligned}$$

as the base value is 100 MVA

$$\begin{aligned} P_{G1}&=\frac{1}{5} \times 100=20MW\\ \Rightarrow \; P_L&=0.5P_{G1}^2\\ &=0.5\left ( \frac{1}{5} \right )^2=0.02p.u.\\ \Rightarrow \; P_L&=0.02 \times 100=2MW\\ P_D&=P_{G1}+P_{G2}-P_L\\ 40&=20+P_{G2}-2\\ \Rightarrow \;\;P_{G2}&=22 MV \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

ee:2012:q26.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 26
ee:2012:q26.question:
Given that
$$A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 &-3 \\ 2&0 \end{bmatrix} \; and \; I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}$$, the value of $A^{3}$ is

detailed_solution.markdown:
$$A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 & -3\\ 2& 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Characteristic equation of A is

$$\begin{bmatrix} -5-\lambda & -3\\ 2& 0-\lambda \end{bmatrix}=0$$

$(-5-\lambda )(-\lambda )+6=0$

$\Rightarrow \;\; \lambda ^2+5\lambda +6=0$

$\text{So,  } A^2+5A+6I=0$

(by Cayley Hamilton theorem)

$\Rightarrow \;\; A^2=-5A-6I$

Multiplying by A on both sides, we have,

$A^3=-5A^2-6A$

$\Rightarrow \;\; A^3=-5(-5A-6I)-6A=19A+30I$

Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

ee:2012:q27.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 27
ee:2012:q27.question: The maximum value of $f(x)=x^{3}-9x^{2}+24x+5$ in the interval [1,6] is

$f(x)=x^3-9x^2+24x+5$ in the interval of [1,6]

First find local maximum if any by putting f'(x)=0.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &=3x^2-18x+24=0 \\ x^2-6x+8&=0 \\ x&=2,4 \\ \text{Now } f''(x) &=6x-18 \\ f''(2)&=12-18=-6 \lt 0 \\ \text{(So } x&=2 \text{ is a point of local maximum)} \\ f''(4)&=24-18=+6 \gt 0 \\ \text{(So } x&=4 \text{ is a point of local minimum)} \\ \end{aligned}$$

Now tabulate the value of f at end point of interval and at local maximum point, to find absolute maximum in given range, as shown below

$$\begin{matrix} x& f(x)\\ 1& 21\\ 2 & 25\\ 6& 41 \end{matrix}$$

Clearly the absolute maxima is at x=6 and absolute maximum value is 41.

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

ee:2012:q31.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 31
ee:2012:q31.question: Let y[n] denote the convolution of h[n] and g[n], where h[n]=$(1/2)^{n}$u[n] and g[n] is a causal sequence. If y[0]=1 and y[1]=1/2, then g[1] equals

detailed_solution.concept: Signals and Systems - Linear Time Invariant Systems
detailed_solution.markdown:
Given, g[n] is causal sequence

Therefore, g[n] will be zero for $n \lt 0$

$$\begin{aligned} y[n]&=\sum_{k=-\infty }^{\infty }g[k]h[n-k]\\ h[n]&=\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )^n u[n]\\ h[n]&=\left\{\begin{matrix} \left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )^n \; ;& n\geq 0\\ 0& n \lt 0 \end{matrix}\right.\\ h[0]&=0, h[1]=\frac{1}{2}, h[2]=\frac{1}{4}\\ y[0]&=g[0] h[0]+g[1]h[-1]+...\\ 1&=g[0] \times 1+0+0+...\\ g[0]&=1\\ y[1]&=g[0]h[1]+g[1]h[0]+g[2]h[-1]+...\\ \frac{1}{2}&=1\cdot \frac{1}{2}+g[1]\cdot 1+0\\ \Rightarrow \;g[1]&=0 \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

ee:2012:q38.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 38
ee:2012:q38.question: The direction of vector A is radially outward from the origin, with $|A|=kr^{n}$, where $r^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}$ and k is a constant. The value of n for which $\bigtriangledown \cdot A= 0$ is

detailed_solution.concept: Electromagnetic Fields - Coordinate Systems and Vector Calculus
detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{aligned} \vec{A} &=kr^n\hat{i}_r \\ \triangledown \cdot \vec{A} &= \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}(r^2 k r^n)\\ &=\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}( k r^{n+2}) \\ &= (n+2)k\frac{r^{n+1}}{r^2}\\ &= (n+2)kr^{n-1}\\ \text{For}\;\; \triangledown \cdot \vec{A} &= 0\\ n+2 &=0\\ \Rightarrow \;\; n=-2 \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

ee:2012:q39.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 39
ee:2012:q39.question:
Consider the differential equation
$\frac{d^{2}y(t)}{dt^{2}}+2\frac{dy(t)}{dt}+y(t)=\delta (t)$ with $y(t)|_{t=0^{-}}=-2$ and $\frac{dy}{dt}|_{t=0^{-}}=0$
The numerical value of $\frac{dy}{dt}|_{t=0^{+}}$, is

detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{aligned} &\frac{d^2y(t)}{dt^2}+2\frac{dy(t)}{dt}+y(t)=\delta (t)\\ &\Rightarrow \; s^2y(s)-sy(0)-y'(0)+2[sy(s)-y(0)]\\&+y(s)=1\\ &\Rightarrow \; y(s)[s^22s+1]-(s \times -2)-y(0)\\&-(2 \times -2)=1\\ &\Rightarrow \; y(s)[s^2+2a+1]=-2s-3\\ &\Rightarrow \;y(s)=\frac{-2s-3}{s^2+2s+1}=\frac{-2}{s+1}-\frac{1}{(s+1)^2}\\ &\Rightarrow \; y(t)=-2e^{-t}-te^{-t}\\ &\frac{dy(t)}{dt}=2e^{-t}-(-te^{-t}+e^{-t})\\ &\frac{dy(t)}{dt}=e^{-t}+te^{-t}\\ &\frac{dy(t)}{dt}|_{t=0^+}=1+0=1 \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **D**.

ee:2012:q41.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 41
ee:2012:q41.question:
The state variable description of an LTI system is given by
$$\begin{pmatrix} \dot{x_{1}}\\ \dot{x_{2}}\\ \dot{x_{3}} \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & a_{1}&0 \\ 0& 0& a_{2}\\ a_{3}& 0& 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2}\\ x_{3} \end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 1 \end{pmatrix}u$$

$$y=(1 \;\;0\;\; 0)\begin{pmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2}\\ x_{3} \end{pmatrix}$$
where y is the output and u is the input. The system is controllable for

detailed_solution.markdown:
$$A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &a_1 &0 \\ 0 & 0& a_2\\ a_3& 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},$$  $$B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix},$$  $$C=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}^T$$

For stable system to be controllable, the metric $Q_c$ must be non singular.

$$Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} B & AB & A^2B \end{bmatrix}$$

$$Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & a_1a_2\\ 0& a_2 &0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

$|Q_c|=-a_1a_2^2$

For $Q_c$ to be nonsingular

ee:2012:q42.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 42
ee:2012:q42.question: The Fourier transform of a signal h(t) is $H(j \omega)=(2\cos\omega)(\sin 2 \omega)/\omega$. The value of h(0) is

detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{aligned} H(j\omega )&=\cos \omega \cdot \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega }\\ &=\frac{e^{j\omega}+e^{-j\omega}}{2}\cdot \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega }\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left [ e^{j\omega}\left ( \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega } \right )+e^{-j\omega}\left ( \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega } \right ) \right ]\\ \text{Let, }X(\omega )&=\frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega } \\ \text{Then, }x(t)&=\left\{\begin{matrix} 1 & -2 \lt t \lt 2\\ 0 & \text{ otherwise} \end{matrix}\right. \\ &\text{By time shifting property}\\ h(t)&=\frac{1}{2}(x(t+1)+x(t-1))\\ \therefore \; h(0)&=\frac{1}{2}[x(1)+x(-1)]=\frac{1}{2}[1+1]=1 \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

ee:2012:q44.title: GATE EE 2012 | Set 1 | Question: 44
ee:2012:q44.question: The input x(t) and output y(t) of a system are related as $y(t)=\int^{t}_{-\infty }x(\tau ) cos (3\tau )d\tau$. The system is

detailed_solution.concept: Signals and Systems - Linear Time Invariant Systems
detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\int_{-\infty }^{t}x{\tau } \cos (3\tau )d\tau \\ y(t-t_0)&=\int_{-\infty }^{t-t_0}x{\tau } \cos (3\tau )d\tau\\ y(t) & \text{ for input }x(t-t_0) \text{ is}\\ y'(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{t}x{\tau -t_0} \cos (3\tau )d\tau\\ y'(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{t-t_0}x{\tau} \cos 3(\tau +t_0 )d\tau\\ y'(t) &\neq y(t-t_0) \end{aligned}$$

So, system is not time invariant for input $x{\tau } =\cos (3\tau )$ bounded input

$y(t)=\int_{-\infty }^{t} \cos ^2 (3\tau )d\tau \rightarrow \infty \; as \; t \rightarrow \infty$

So, for bounded input, output is not bounded therefore system is not stable.

Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.
